headline: Australia Working Holiday Visa 2026: Subclass 417 Requirements and Costs
metaDescription: Australia Working Holiday visa 2026: subclass 417 rules, age 18-30 (35 for some), AUD 840 fee, AUD 5,000 funds and how to extend for a second year.

sections.content:
The Working Holiday visa (subclass 417) is how hundreds of thousands of young travellers fund their Australian adventure. It lets passport holders from 19 eligible countries live and work in Australia for up to 12 months, with the option to extend for a second and third year by completing specified work in regional Australia. There is no annual cap — if you meet the criteria, you can apply at any time.

The headline rules for 2026: you must be 18 to 30 when you apply, or 18 to 35 if you hold a Canadian, French, Irish or British passport — extended since 1 July 2026 to German, Cypriot, Finnish and South Korean passports too. You need around AUD 5,000 in funds plus enough for a fare out, no dependent children accompanying you, and you must satisfy health and character requirements.
sections.title: What the Subclass 417 Visa Offers

sections.content:
The base application charge is AUD 840 for your first Working Holiday visa, with second and third visas costing AUD 1,000 each. Fees are set by the Department of Home Affairs, indexed each July — the current charges date from 1 July 2026 — so verify the figure on the official Visa Pricing Estimator before paying.

Once granted, you can enter Australia any time within 12 months of the grant, and your 12-month stay starts the day you arrive, with unlimited entries and exits. You can work for any employer but generally no more than six months with one employer, and you may study for up to four months. Processing is currently running at around three months, so do not book flights until the visa is granted.
sections.title: Costs, Stay Rules and Processing

sections.content:
Extending is where the 417 rewards regional workers. A second-year visa requires 88 days of specified work in regional Australia during your first visa — industries like farming, mining, construction and fishing qualify, and the Department checks payslips, employer ABNs and dates, so keep records as you go. A third-year visa needs six months of specified work while on the second visa.

British passport holders get a major concession under the Australia-UK Free Trade Agreement: since 1 July 2024 they can be granted up to three Working Holiday visas without completing any specified regional work. Everyone else still needs the days, so plan your first year with the second visa in mind if you want to stay.
sections.title: Second and Third Year Extensions

sections.content:
In September 2026 the Minister for Home Affairs announced a significant proposed change: second and third Working Holiday Maker visas would move to a capped ballot, with 45,000 second-year places a year — down from about 57,000 granted the previous year — and just 5,000 third-year places. Specified work would qualify you to enter the ballot rather than guaranteeing the visa.

Crucially, the regulation to enact this had not been made when the announcement was published, so the current uncapped rules still apply. The Government also said it would stabilise processing at about three months. If you are planning around a second or third visa, check the Home Affairs website for the latest position before making irreversible plans.
